title: The infinitive construct and the infinitive absolute

objectives.can: Tell the infinitive construct from the infinitive absolute and name the commonest use of each.

explanation.summary: Hebrew has two infinitives, and they do different jobs. The infinitive construct is a verbal noun that is joined to prepositions and suffixes: 'to keep', 'when he came', 'your eating'. The infinitive absolute is a bare, unchanging form that is used for emphasis, for a command or as an adverb.

sections.heading: The infinitive construct
body: The infinitive construct names the action as a thing, a verbal noun. Like a noun in the construct state, it is bound closely to what follows it, and like a noun it may have a preposition on the front and a pronominal suffix at the end. Its shape in the Qal of a strong verb is that of the masculine singular imperative: שְׁמֹר. The word-by-word display gives it the features HebForm=infinitive-construct and, when they are present, Prefix and Suffix.

The commonest preposition on it is לְ. It gives the sense 'to …', as in לִשְׁמֹר 'to keep' (a purpose, or what someone is told or able to do). With בְּ or כְּ the infinitive makes a time clause: בִּשְׁמוֹר 'in keeping' or, more freely, 'when he kept'; כְּבוֹא 'when he came'. A negative infinitive is made with בִּלְתִּי: 'not to eat'.

A suffix on the infinitive can be the subject or the object of the action. In אֲכָלְךָ the suffix is the subject: 'your eating', 'when you eat'. In לְעָבְדָהּ the suffix is the object: 'to work it'. Read the clause to decide which it is.

head: Form
Infinitive construct
Infinitive absolute
rows: Shape in the Qal of a strong verb
after a preposition: purpose, time, object of another verb
before its own verb for emphasis; as a command; as an adverb

sections.heading: The infinitive absolute
body: The infinitive absolute has a fixed shape, in the Qal usually with ō as the vowel of the second syllable: שָׁמוֹר. It takes no suffix and does not combine with prepositions. It does not say who acts or when; the sentence round it supplies that.

Its commonest use is to stand beside a finite verb of the same root, usually just before it. It then strengthens the verb, and a good English rendering might be 'surely', 'indeed' or 'without fail'. This is not a mechanical formula; the strength it adds may be certainty, intensity or contrast, and the context tells which. In Genesis 2:17 and 3:4, the pair מוֹת תָּמוּת stands in the warning and the denial. In Genesis 37:8 the brothers use it in a question: 'will you indeed reign over us?'

It can also continue an action after a finite verb, as in הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב in Genesis 8:3, where the pair of infinitives tells how the waters went back, 'going and returning', which English may render 'continually'. And it can stand alone as a command. In Deuteronomy 5:12 the command to keep the sabbath is put in the infinitive absolute, שָׁמוֹר, where a masculine singular imperative would also have been possible.

sections.heading: Telling the two apart
body: Look first at the word's neighbours. A preposition or a suffix means a construct infinitive. A form standing next to a finite verb of the same root, or in front of a clause as a command, is probably an absolute. The vowels help in the Qal of a strong verb: the construct infinitive has the same shape as the masculine singular imperative, while the absolute usually has ā in the first syllable and ō in the second.
In weak verbs the two forms can look much alike, and then the context counts for more than the letters.

misunderstandings: The two infinitives are not two spellings of one form. They have different jobs: one is a verbal noun, the other an emphasising or adverbial form.
An infinitive does not carry a tense or a person. 'To keep' in Hebrew says nothing about when or by whom; the clause tells you that.

An infinitive construct with לְ is not always a purpose clause. It can also complete another verb, as the object of what someone says or can do, or stand as the subject or predicate of a clause. Read the whole clause.
A pair such as מוֹת תָּמוּת is not a mistake or a repeated word. The first member is the infinitive absolute, the second a finite verb, and together they add force to the statement.

deeper.heading: The infinitive absolute in other uses
body: The infinitive absolute sometimes stands where a finite verb might be expected, as in a series of commands or in the narration of a series of actions. It has long been discussed whether it is best called a verbal noun or an adverbial form. The grammars describe its uses as emphasis, command and continuation, and that is a safe way to read it.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Both infinitives in one verse. אֲכָלְךָ is an infinitive construct with the suffix of the second person, after the preposition בְּ of בְּיוֹם: 'in the day of your eating'. מוֹת is an infinitive absolute standing before the finite verb תָּמוּת from the same root: the pair is a warning, 'you will surely die'. The suffix and the preposition mark the first, and the bare form next to the finite verb marks the second.

examples.analysis: כְּבוֹא is an infinitive construct of בּוֹא 'come', with כְּ in front. The infinitive gives a time clause: 'when Abram came into Egypt'. The subject, Abram, stands right after the infinitive in the way that a noun stands after a noun in the construct state.

quoted.title: Genesis

examples.analysis: לְעָבְדָהּ and וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ are infinitives construct with לְ and the suffix of 'her': 'to work it and to keep it'. The suffix is the object of the action, and the infinitives tell what the man was put in the garden to do.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the waters returned from off the earth continually; and after the end of a hundred and fifty days the waters decreased.

examples.analysis: הָלוֹךְ and וָשׁוֹב are two infinitives absolute, 'going' and 'returning', joined by וְ. They stand after the finite verb וַיָּשֻׁבוּ and say how the waters withdrew, steadily and continually. They do not take a person or a tense: the finite verb supplies those.

quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It negates the construct infinitive: 'not to eat'
It adds a suffix to the infinitive
It turns the infinitive into a noun
check.explain: בִּלְתִּי is the negative word for infinitives. The infinitive after it is a construct infinitive; the preposition לְ is attached to בִּלְתִּי.

check.prompt: What does the first word do in הֲמָלֹךְ תִּמְלֹךְ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And his brethren said to him: 'Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?' And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is an infinitive absolute that strengthens the finite verb in a question: 'will you indeed reign?'
It is a construct infinitive meaning 'to reign' after a preposition
check.explain: The first word has the ה of the question on the front. The infinitive absolute stands before its own finite verb תִּמְלֹךְ and adds weight to the question.

check.prompt: How does the infinitive אֲכָלְךָ work in the clause?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The suffix is its object: 'to eat you'
The suffix is its subject: 'in the day of your eating'
It is a command to the man
check.explain: The man is the one who eats, so the suffix of the second person is the subject of the infinitive. The preposition בְּ is on the noun יוֹם before it.

reading.why: Within a few verses the garden story uses infinitives construct for purpose and with suffixes, an infinitive absolute with a finite verb in the warning, and an infinitive construct as the subject of a verbless clause.
